answers.solution:
According to the author, a successful leader leads by example and communicates well with his teammates. He takes the right decisions, motivates everyone to give their best, remains calm in times of crisis and out-thinks his opponents. Many people also judge him by the number of trophies he wins.

(From the second paragraph: 'a successful leader distinguishes himself by being able to lead by example ...')
answers.finalAnswer: A successful leader leads by example, communicates well with teammates, takes the right decisions, motivates everyone, stays calm in a crisis and out-thinks rivals.

answers.solution:
A great leader believes that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. He accepts defeat with dignity and celebrates victory decently, and he always respects others. He sacrifices personal glory for the team's success, and he does not despise failure but treats it as his teacher.

(From the second half of the second paragraph.)
answers.finalAnswer: He believes the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, accepts defeat with dignity and celebrates victory decently, respects others, puts the team's glory above his own and learns from failure.

answers.solution: A successful leader has the skills of leadership and wins matches and trophies, but he lacks something a great leader has. A great leader puts the team above himself, stays dignified in both defeat and victory, respects others and learns from his failures.
answers.finalAnswer: A successful leader has good leadership skills and wins; a great leader also puts the team above himself, stays dignified in defeat and victory, and learns from failure.

answers.solution: The author groups captains by what they are known for. Some are popular for their looks, humour or cheerful nature; some are famous for personal milestones; some are remembered for trophies; some are controversial for being aggressive; some are notorious for self-importance; some are respected for honouring the rules; and some stand out for quick thinking.
answers.finalAnswer: Popular for looks, humour or cheerfulness; famous for personal milestones; remembered for trophies; controversial for aggression; notorious for self-importance; respected for honouring the rules; marked out by quick thinking.

answers.solution: (Any five good qualities may be given.) As a leader, I would love to lead by example, communicate clearly with my team, take the right decisions, remain calm in a crisis and respect everyone, whether we win or lose. I would also treat failure as my teacher.
answers.finalAnswer: Leading by example; good communication; right decisions; calmness in a crisis; respect for others

answers.solution: The phone can do countless things: show TV, weather and the internet, check blood pressure, take photos and guide him home. The poet, however, cannot even work out how to make a simple phone call on it, so he feels the phone is smarter than he is.
answers.finalAnswer: The phone can do countless things, yet the poet cannot even work out how to make a simple call on it.

answers.solution: The phone can check his blood pressure and temperature "without even probing all my apertures", that is, without any examination of his body. The poet could never have imagined a phone doing that.
answers.finalAnswer: It can check his blood pressure and temperature without examining his body.

answers.solution: The poet's 'Eureka moment' comes when he discovers the phone has a camera: 'A camera..... a CAMERA! Now I can take shots'. He is excited that he can now click photos of everyone and even take a 'selfie'.
answers.finalAnswer: Discovering that the phone has a camera, so he can take photos and selfies.

answers.solution: Mr. Bell is Alexander Graham Bell, who invented the telephone. The poet refers to him because the inventor himself would be amazed to see how many things a phone can do today.
answers.finalAnswer: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone; he would be amazed at what it has become.

answers.solution: The poet worries that, with all its gadgets and features, he still does not know how to do the simplest thing: make a phone call. (He also notes how costly the phone is.)
answers.finalAnswer: Despite all its gadgets, he does not know how to make a simple phone call on it.

answers.solution:
(i) gadgets: **gizmos** ("Despite all the gizmos that strike me with awe")
(ii) to examine: **probing** ("Without even probing all my apertures")
answers.finalAnswer: (i) gizmos; (ii) probing

answers.solution: It is a **metaphor**. A question cannot really be stuck in the throat (a 'craw' is a bird's throat); the poet compares a doubt he cannot get rid of to something stuck in his throat, without using 'like' or 'as'.
answers.finalAnswer: Metaphor

answers.solution: A suitable title: **"Smart Phone, Not-So-Smart Me"** (or "My Smart Phone"), because the poem is about a phone that can do everything and an owner who cannot even make a call on it.
answers.finalAnswer: Smart Phone, Not-So-Smart Me

answers.solution: Two pairs of rhyming words: **Greece - geese** and **Bell - tell**. (Others: not - got, too - do, shoot - hoot, awe - craw, all - call.)
answers.finalAnswer: Greece - geese; Bell - tell

**Online Learning is the Future of Education**
by Aarav Sharma

When schools closed during the pandemic, learning did not stop. It simply moved online.

Online learning lets a student learn anywhere and at any time. A child in a small village can watch a lesson by the best teacher in the country. Recorded classes can be paused and replayed until a topic is clear, and quizzes give instant results.

However, online learning cannot do everything. Many students do not have a good phone or internet, and long hours on a screen tire the eyes. Sports, friendship and discipline are best learnt in a real school.

So the future of education will be a blend: online tools that support the classroom, not replace it.

The Editor
The Times of India
New Delhi

Subject: Harm done by cheap notes and guides

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw attention to the harm that cheap notes and guides are doing to students.

Many students no longer read their textbooks. They simply memorise ready-made answers from these guides before examinations. As a result, they do not understand the concepts and cannot think or write on their own. Many of these guides are also full of mistakes, which students learn as facts. Parents waste money on them, and the habit of hard work slowly dies.

I request teachers and parents to discourage the use of such guides, and the authorities to check their sale.

Yours faithfully,
Aarav Sharma

**Toofan Finds His Way Home**

Raju's father owned a white horse named Toofan, the fastest horse in the village. One stormy night, thunder frightened Toofan. He broke his rope and galloped away into the darkness. Raju cried all night, and in the morning the villagers searched the forest, but there was no sign of him.

Three days later, late at night, a fire broke out on the hill near the village. Suddenly the villagers heard loud hooves. Toofan came galloping down the hill, his mane flying, neighing loudly to wake everyone. The villagers rushed out with buckets of water and put out the fire before it reached their homes.

Raju hugged Toofan tightly. From that day, everyone called him the hero of the village.

answers.solution:
1. He and I **were** playing. (Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.)
2. English as well as Urdu **is** taught here. (The verb agrees with the first subject.)
3. Neither of the two men **was** very strong. ('Neither' is singular.)
4. Ten kilometres **is** a long walk. (A distance taken as one amount is singular.)
5. No news **is** good news. ('News' is singular.)
6. Many a man **has** done so. ('Many a' takes a singular verb.)
7. The quality of the mangoes **was** not good. (The subject is 'quality'.)
8. Two-third of the city **is** in ruins. (A fraction of a singular noun takes a singular verb.)
9. The United States **has** a big navy. (The name of one country is singular.)
10. The ship with its members **was** lost. (The subject is 'the ship'; 'with its members' does not change it.)

Note: as printed, the parts are labelled (a), (b), (a), (b), (c) ... (h), and 'Two-third' should read 'Two-thirds'.
answers.finalAnswer: were; is; was; is; is; has; was; is; has; was
answers.notice: The parts are printed (a), (b), then (a), (b), (c) and on; there are ten sentences, answered in order.
